query: Refractory high-entropy alloys are promising structural materials, but achieving a strong combination of strength and plasticity remains important. What single intervention could improve this strength–plasticity combination? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an appropriate reference alloy, the conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a dilute concentration of interstitial carbon (around 0.3 at.%) into a Nb‐based refractory high-entropy alloy, combined with an intermediate annealing treatment that encourages the formation of discrete, nanoscale carbide precipitates within a continuous ductile BCC matrix, will enhance both yield strength (via precipitation strengthening) and ductility (by preserving matrix connectivity) compared to the undoped baseline alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A Nb‐based refractory HEA (e.g., one with composition NbTaTiV or a similar refractory alloy without significant interstitial content) in a predominantly disordered BCC matrix.
generation.intervention: Introduce a dilute interstitial carbon addition (≈0.3 at.%) during alloy synthesis and apply a tailored thermal treatment (solutionizing followed by an intermediate annealing at moderate temperature, e.g., ~600 °C) to promote the nucleation of discrete, nanoscale carbides.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature mechanical testing (and up to ~700 °C) under standard tensile and compression tests; processing parameters chosen to avoid high-pressure or excessive carbide coarsening conditions that might lead to continuous carbide networks.
generation.structural_mediator: Uniformly dispersed nanoscale carbide particles (e.g., Nb3C or Ta3C-type carbides) that are coherently embedded in a continuous, ductile BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The interstitial carbon facilitates the controlled formation of fine carbide precipitates. These carbides serve as obstacles to dislocation motion, providing precipitation strengthening without interrupting the continuity of the ductile matrix. The discrete nature of the precipitates minimizes the brittleness associated with continuous hard phases, thereby maintaining or even improving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline undoped alloy, the carbon-doped alloy should exhibit a significant increase in yield strength (predicted on the order of ~15–20% improvement, though the precise increase is uncertain) while either maintaining or moderately enhancing ductility. This synergy should be maintained at both room and moderately elevated temperatures (up to ~700 °C).
generation.baseline: The same Nb‐based refractory HEA processed identically but without any carbon addition, where typically high strength is achieved at the expense of plasticity due to the continuous nature of the BCC matrix.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected under moderate annealing conditions that avoid high-pressure environments or excessive carbide coalescence; the approach is aimed at refractory HEAs with a similar phase stability and BCC-dominant microstructure. Different alloy systems or processing windows that lead to continuous carbide networks may not show the desired improvements.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the findings from PMC7517255 (which demonstrated that low-level carbon doping can induce carbide formation under high-pressure/high-temperature conditions) and PMC5227964 (which reported interstitial carbon aiding strengthening in HEAs) into a Nb-based refractory HEA system using optimized thermal processing. The uncertainty lies in controlling carbide morphology under ambient-pressure conditions and ensuring that discrete carbide formation (rather than a network) is achieved in this new system.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of Nb‐based refractory HEA samples with identical base compositions and processing routes. One set is doped with 0.3 at.% carbon and the other serves as the carbon-free baseline. After homogenization (solution treatment), apply an intermediate annealing treatment (e.g., 600 °C for an optimized duration) designed to induce discrete carbide precipitation. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and APT to verify the presence and distribution of nanoscale carbides. Subsequently, conduct standardized tensile and compression tests at room temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 600 °C). Compare the yield strength and ductility metrics between the doped and undoped samples.
measurements: TEM and APT for carbide size, number density, and dispersion
Tensile yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and ductility (% elongation)
Compression tests for yield strength and plastic strain
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in yield strength (target improvement >15%) while maintaining or improving ductility compared to the undoped baseline, or if the carbide precipitates form continuous networks rather than discrete particles, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The improved mechanical properties (Fig. 3) and the associated multiple deformation mechanisms (Fig. 4) confirm the success of the new design approach, and its potential economic viability since interstitial alloying elements are much cheaper compared to substitutional alloying elements. The new interstitial TWIP-TRIP-HEAs unify all known metallurgical strengthening effects in one single bulk material: i) massive substitutional solid solution strengthening due to multiple principle elements (i.e., Fe, Mn, Co and Cr); ii) interstitial solid solution strengthening by carbon; iii) micro-composite effect from dual-phase structure; iv) nano-particle strengthening from nano-carbides (Figs 2b and 4c); v) nano-twinning induced plasticity effect (TWIP) (Fig. 4b); vi) displacive transformation induced plasticity effect (TRIP) (Fig. 4a); vii) formation of stacking faults (Fig. 4b); viii) grain size reduction (increased grain boundary density); and dislocation hardening (Fig. 4b).

In this work, the effect of dilute C-doped with a concertation of 0.1 at.% in RHEA master alloy was studied under both ambient pressure and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. Under low pressure, the XRD of RHEA with/without C shows the formation of pure BCC phase and lattice constant of 3.210 Å, indicating that the low concertation of C has an ignorable effect on the alloy phase and the crystal structure of RHEA. However, the doping of C has noticeable a impact on the hardness values of the RHEA. At a high pressure of 6 GPa, Ta3C and Nb3C Carbide with FCC_L12 phase appear when the temperature is above 809 °C. The carbides of Ta3C and Nb3C are very stable even when temperature increased to above 1000 °C. As carbides are usually shown and favorable in high-temperature structural materials in the form of hard constitutes in metal matrix composites, the mechanical properties of carbon doped master alloy RHEA might be improved after a combined high-pressure and high-temperature process.
